title: Praying for the dead, again
hook: the communion between living and dead isn't broken
tomorrow: if the body is buried, why does the Creed end with it?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was love continues: grief is love with nowhere to go, and it keeps its own time. Today, one place that love can still go.

A friend's grandpa dies. His family isn't religious. Can you still pray for him? An old story asks nearly the same question. A battle is over. The next day Judas Maccabeus and his men go out to carry home their dead. Under the coats of the fallen they find small charms from the idols of Jamnia, things their law forbade. These men died holding exactly what they shouldn't have. So what does Judas do?
screen: `CAN YOU STILL PRAY FOR HIM?` → `AFTER THE BATTLE.` → `CHARMS UNDER THEIR COATS.`

segments.voice: He doesn't write them off. Second Maccabees says Judas and his men turned to prayer, asking that the sin be blotted out. Then they took up a collection and sent it to Jerusalem for a sacrifice for the dead, because, the writer says, they hoped the dead would rise. His verdict, in the Douay-Rheims: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead." Notice who they prayed for. Not heroes. Men who died with the wrong thing in their pockets. Paul gives the reason this works: "whether we live, or whether we die, we are the Lord's." Death moves someone, but not out of God's hands, so it doesn't cut the line between us. The Church calls that line the communion of saints: the living, the dead being made ready for God, and the saints in heaven, still one family. A preface said at Masses for the dead puts it in four Latin words: vita mutatur, non tollitur. Life is changed, not taken away. One to tell a friend: one of the Mass's Eucharistic Prayers remembers all the dead whose faith God alone has known. It doesn't check anyone's paperwork first. That's why the Church still prays for the dead at every Mass, by name when it can, and leaves the judging to God.
screen: `JUDAS PRAYS FOR THE FALLEN.` · `A HOLY AND WHOLESOME THOUGHT.` · `WE ARE THE LORD'S.` · `LIFE IS CHANGED, NOT TAKEN AWAY.` · then, large: `NOT BROKEN.`

segments.voice: Say one name out loud, someone who has died: family, a friend, a friend's grandparent you barely knew. Hold the name for a few breaths, as if it were still a conversation. If you pray, the old words are these: eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon them.
Praying for the dead. Love spoken as prayer for those who have died, because death doesn't cut the line.
Your line: not broken. The dead are still family, and prayer still reaches them. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1723 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: IF THE BODY IS BURIED, WHY DOES THE CREED END WITH IT?`

howItsDone: Catholics pray for the dead at every Mass, have Masses offered for them, and pray the Eternal Rest prayer, especially in November and on the anniversary of a death.

Preface I for the Dead: 'vita mutatur, non tollitur' quoted in Latin; confirm. 'Four Latin words' counts vita, mutatur, non, tollitur.
